open-question.question: Codex's plugin documentation describes a root plugin.json as the portable manifest and .codex-plugin/plugin.json as a compatibility fallback, while every plugin in Codex's own curated marketplace keeps its manifest at .codex-plugin/plugin.json and none keeps one at the plugin root. Where should the Codex host tree keep its plugin manifest?

Claude Code users install cairn by adding the distribution repository as a marketplace, and Antigravity users by extracting it into a fixed workspace directory. Codex offers `codex plugin marketplace add <owner/repo>` followed by `codex plugin add <plugin>@<marketplace>`, and its curated marketplace declares itself in a .agents/plugins/marketplace.json file. By what route should a Codex user install cairn from the uHappyLogic/cairn-codex repository?

Every rendered skill, agent, and shared procedure reaches the plugin's Python tools and shared procedures through a per-host literal that replaces the {{PLUGIN_ROOT}} placeholder: an environment variable on Claude Code, a workspace-relative path on Antigravity. Codex's documentation names a PLUGIN_ROOT environment variable, but nothing yet shows that it is set for the shell commands a skill runs or inside a subagent. What literal should the Codex host definition use for the plugin root?

Cairn's two dispatched agents are Markdown files with YAML frontmatter under the plugin's agents/ directory. Codex defines custom subagents as TOML files (name, description, developer_instructions) looked up in the project's .codex/agents/ or the user's ~/.codex/agents/, its documentation does not say a plugin can ship them, and no plugin in its curated marketplace ships one. On Codex, in what form should the plugin carry each agent's instructions, and by what step, if any, should they become subagents a cairn skill can spawn?

The runtime layer under core/ is written once for every host, and the build applies only three text operations to it: plugin-root replacement, regex deletion, and frontmatter key stripping. Where a core/ sentence cannot read the same on Codex as on the other hosts, for example the two dispatch sites that name the Agent tool and a cairn:<agent> registry name, by what mechanism should the difference reach the Codex tree?
open-question.alternative: The build gets no new mechanism. Neither core/ nor any host definition carries a per-host variant, so the Codex tree renders the same dispatch sentences as the other two hosts, naming the `Agent` tool, `subagent_type`, the `cairn:<agent>` registry name, and "the agent id the `Agent` tool returned". The Codex runner has to map that wording onto its own subagent-spawning facility. Nothing changes in core/, in build_hosts.py's fixed settings key set, or in the Claude Code and Antigravity trees. The build keeps its three text operations, and no machinery is added before a live Codex run shows that it is needed. The Codex tree tells the runner to call a tool and pass a registry name that may not exist on Codex. Whether a dispatch then succeeds depends on how the model reads the sentence, and the milestone's goal requires both agents to run as Codex subagents. Whether this works at all depends on the axis the agent-form-and-registration question owns: how a Codex agent is named and spawned.

This rejects the premise that the sentence cannot read the same on every host. Each such core/ sentence is rewritten once in capability terms, for example "dispatch the `complete-task` agent of this plugin as a subagent, with a prompt containing only…" and "a follow-up message to the same subagent where the host can continue one". Specific tool names, parameter names, and registry names are dropped. The build and every host definition stay as they are, and all three trees render the new wording. It follows the existing invariant that host-dependent sentences name the capability, never the host. It keeps one text per site with no variants to keep in sync, and it needs no build change or per-host data. The Claude Code and Antigravity trees lose the exact `Agent`/`subagent_type`/`cairn:<agent>` instruction that reliably steers their runners today, so their dispatch text changes and their behaviour has to be re-shown. Whether that is allowed depends on the bar the existing-host preservation question owns. Neutral wording also works on Codex only if Codex can spawn the agent from a description rather than a precise name, which the agent-form question owns.

core/ holds each differing sentence in every host's variant, wrapped in host-neutral capability markers, for example markers keyed to a registry-name dispatch versus a named-subagent dispatch, since core/ may not name a host. Each host definition's existing `prose_drop_patterns` regexes delete the variants that do not apply, along with every marker. The build gains no new operation. The Claude Code and Antigravity definitions gain drop patterns, and their rendered text can stay byte-identical to today's. It needs only an operation the build already has, needs no change to build_hosts.py or its settings key set, and keeps every host's wording side by side in the one core/ file where an editor sees it. core/ files become harder to read, with interleaved variants and markers. Every host definition has to keep a regex set in step with the markers. A malformed or missed marker either leaks a foreign variant into a tree or deletes too much text, and no existing check catches either.

The build gains a new operation: core/ carries named placeholder slots, in the style of `{{PLUGIN_ROOT}}`, at each sentence or phrase that differs, and a new settings key holds each host's value for every slot. All three host definitions declare every slot. The Claude Code and Antigravity values are today's exact wording, so their trees can render byte-identically. The existing unfilled-placeholder check catches a slot a host fails to fill. Each variation point is explicit and named in core/, every host has to supply it, and a missing value fails the build. It extends the one substitution pattern the build already trusts and scales to later differences such as the context-file name or the skill invocation form. It changes build_hosts.py's fixed key set and every host's settings.toml. It splits sentences between core/ and three settings files, so a core/ editor can no longer read the full instruction in one place. Multi-line values in TOML are awkward to maintain. How many sites it ends up serving depends on how the context-file and skill-invocation questions settle.

The build gains a new operation: a settings key of literal or regex find-and-replace pairs applied to the rendered text of core/ files. Only the Codex definition declares pairs, which rewrite the `Agent`-tool dispatch sentences and the agent-id repair clause into Codex's form. core/ and the other two definitions are untouched apart from an empty key, so their trees stay byte-identical. core/ keeps a single readable text with no markers or slots, and the Claude Code and Antigravity trees are guaranteed unchanged. All of Codex's differences sit in one place in its own definition. The rules match against core/ wording that an editor of core/ cannot see is depended on. A later rewording silently stops matching and leaves the Codex tree wrong, unless the build also gains a check that every rule matched. Adding that check is more build code that no test under tests/ covers today.

Each core/ file whose wording differs is excluded from the Codex tree through the existing `exclude` key. A Codex-specific copy of the whole file is shipped as a template under scripts/hosts/codex/ at the same relative path. The build either stays as it is, with the copy hard-coding the Codex plugin-root literal because templates fill only `{{VERSION}}` and `{{NAME}}`, or gains one change that also fills `{{PLUGIN_ROOT}}` in templates. Codex gets complete freedom to restructure a dispatch skill around its own subagent model, for example a different repair branch, rather than swapping phrases. With the hard-coded literal it needs no build change, and the other two trees are untouched. Each overridden skill exists twice, once in core/ and once in the Codex definition, and nothing detects when core/ changes and the copy does not. That reintroduces the hand-kept duplication the host-neutral core/ exists to remove, on the two largest orchestrating skills.

The differing instruction moves out of the skills into a small host-supplied file. core/ says to dispatch by following `{{PLUGIN_ROOT}}/shared/<dispatch file>.md`, and each host definition supplies that file as a template, giving the host's exact tool, name, and follow-up wording. The build needs no new operation, and the existing dangling-plugin-root check fails any host that omits the file. It uses only existing build mechanisms. It keeps the host-specific text to one short, purpose-named file per host, read at runtime, with precise wording on every host instead of capability prose. It keeps the orchestration logic itself single-sourced in core/. The Claude Code and Antigravity dispatch skills change text and gain a read step at every dispatch, so their trees are no longer byte-identical. Whether that is allowed depends on the bar the existing-host preservation question owns. It also stretches `shared/`, which so far holds only procedures referenced by two or more runners, to hold per-host fragments.

open-question.question: Cairn's skills read the project's environment context from CLAUDE.md, the bootstrap skill writes the Milestone Workflow section into it, and finish-current-milestone updates it, while Codex's project instruction file is AGENTS.md. Which file should the Codex tree's skills read and write as the project's context file?

Cairn's skills, READMEs, and docs name every skill in slash form (/skill-name, or /cairn:skill-name under the plugin namespace), while Codex's documentation gives $skillname or the /skills picker as the explicit invocation, and nothing yet shows how Codex names a plugin's skills. In what form should the Codex tree and the Codex installation instructions name cairn's skills?

docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md documents headless chains as `claude -p` or `agy -p` lines, explains each flag per host, and gives a one-line swap between those two binaries. Codex runs non-interactively as `codex exec` with different flag names and no effort flag. How much Codex coverage should that page gain?

Codex ships as a command-line tool, a desktop app, and an IDE extension, and this milestone's live verification runs on the command-line tool only. Which Codex surfaces should the README and the distribution repository say cairn supports?
open-question.alternative: The README and the distribution repository say cairn supports Codex as a host and name none of its surfaces. They make no claim about the command-line tool, the desktop app, or the IDE extension in either direction, and the installation steps are written as whatever commands the chosen install route uses. It matches how the Claude Code and Antigravity READMEs already describe their hosts: neither names a surface, even though Claude Code also ships more than one. The three host sections stay parallel, and nothing has to be revised when Codex adds, renames, or merges a surface. It quietly suggests that every Codex surface works when only the command-line tool is verified live. A desktop-app or IDE-extension user whose plugin install, PLUGIN_ROOT resolution, or subagent dispatch behaves differently has nothing to warn them, and their bug reports arrive without the surface being named.

The README and the distribution repository name the Codex command-line tool as the supported surface. They say nothing about the desktop app or the IDE extension, neither claiming nor ruling them out. Every word of the support claim is backed by this milestone's live verification, and the claim stays short and in step with the CLI-shaped install commands (`codex plugin marketplace add`, `codex plugin add`). Saying nothing about the other two surfaces leaves their users guessing whether silence means untested or unsupported. Naming a surface also breaks the surface-free wording the other two host sections use, so the Codex section reads differently from its siblings.

The README and the distribution repository name the Codex command-line tool as the only supported surface. They state outright that the desktop app and the IDE extension are not supported. It sets the clearest expectations and gives a firm answer to bug reports from surfaces nobody has verified. Desktop-app and IDE-extension failures are kept out of the project's support scope until someone exercises those surfaces. It may turn away users for whom cairn would work as it stands, if those surfaces share the CLI's plugin installation and configuration, which nothing on this machine has confirmed either way. Lifting the exclusion later takes a deliberate README and distribution-repository change plus a release.

The README and the distribution repository name the command-line tool as the supported, verified surface. They name the desktop app and the IDE extension as expected to work but not verified, so the claim has two tiers. It tells every Codex user exactly where things stand: one surface backed by a live run, two that are plausible but untested. Desktop and IDE users are invited to try it and report what they find, without the project promising anything it has not exercised. "Expected to work" is still a soft claim with no evidence behind it, since nothing yet shows the desktop app or IDE extension install plugins or dispatch subagents the way the CLI does. It is also the wordiest option, and once copied verbatim into the root README it is the hardest to keep in step with a fourth host's wording.

The README and the distribution repository say cairn supports all three Codex surfaces as equals: the command-line tool, the desktop app, and the IDE extension. It gives the widest reach and the simplest message for a Codex user on any surface. It fits the goal of making Codex a fully supported host without hedging the public claim. Two of the three claimed surfaces go beyond this milestone's verification, which runs on the CLI only and on a free-tier allowance that leaves no room to exercise the others. If a surface differs in plugin install, PLUGIN_ROOT exposure, or subagent dispatch, the published claim is simply wrong.

open-question.question: Every file-changing cairn skill commits to git and runs python3 tools that live in the installed plugin directory, outside the project workspace, and Codex runs model-issued shell commands under a sandbox and approval policy (read-only, workspace-write, or full access). What sandbox and approval configuration should cairn's Codex instructions tell users to run under?

The alternatives pass dispatches one subagent per open question, all at once where the host allows parallel dispatch and one after another where it does not, with no cap. Codex runs subagents in parallel but limits how many subagent threads a session may hold open at once. How should the pass behave on a host that allows parallel dispatch only up to a limit?

The goal lets core/ and the build change where Codex requires it, provided the Claude Code and Antigravity trees keep their behaviour. By what bar is that judged: must those two rendered trees stay byte-identical, or may their text change, and if it may, what check shows their behaviour is kept?

Several Codex behaviours the design rests on are unverified on this machine: whether PLUGIN_ROOT is set for the commands a skill runs, whether a plugin-shipped agent can be spawned by name, how a plugin's skills are invoked, and whether a finished subagent accepts a follow-up message. The only Codex account available is free tier, so each live run spends a scarce allowance. At what point in the milestone should these behaviours be established by live Codex runs?
open-question.alternative: Live runs come before the design is decided. Once the alternatives and recommendation passes have run, and before any of the dependent sibling questions is answered, a minimal throwaway fixture plugin is installed into Codex. It is not the cairn tree, which does not exist yet. One small live session then probes all four behaviours together: whether PLUGIN_ROOT is set in a skill's shell commands, whether a plugin-shipped agent can be spawned by name, how a plugin skill is invoked, and whether a finished subagent accepts a follow-up message. The results are added to requirements.md's starting state before the dependent questions are answered. Separately, the goal's live verification run still happens at the end of the milestone against the real tree. Every dependent decision (plugin-root literal, agent form and registration, skill invocation form, the repair branch of the alternatives pass) is recorded against observed behaviour rather than documentation the starting state marks as unconfirmed. This avoids the revert-then-re-answer cycles a wrong documented assumption would cause after tasks are derived. It spends free-tier allowance twice, once on the fixture probe and again on the final verification. A fixture plugin is also not the shipped tree, so a behaviour seen on the fixture can still differ on the real cairn tree, and requirements work stalls until a live session can be run.

The dependent sibling questions are answered now on documented behaviour and the evidence from the curated marketplace. derive-tasks puts one probe task at the head of the task list, run against a minimal fixture plugin before any task that builds on the probed behaviours. Any probe result that contradicts a recorded decision is handled by revert-then-re-answer of that decision before the dependent tasks continue. The final live verification run stays at the end of the milestone as the goal specifies. Requirements work goes ahead without waiting on a live session. Yet nothing is built on an unconfirmed behaviour, because the probe still comes before the implementation tasks it gates. Decisions are recorded on assumptions that may be overturned. A contradicting probe means reverting answers and possibly re-deriving tasks. It spends allowance on a separate fixture session as well as on the final run.

alternative.id: Just-in-time probes on the real tree

open-question.alternative: There is no up-front probe session. Each behaviour is checked by a small live run right before, or as part of, the task that depends on it, against the partially built hosts/codex/ tree rather than a fixture. The plugin-root probe runs once the host definition renders. The skill-invocation probe runs once the tree installs. The agent spawn and follow-up probes run once the agent form exists. Decisions are recorded on documented behaviour. The goal's final verification run happens at the end. Each probe exercises the real rendered artifact rather than a stand-in, so a pass is direct evidence for what ships. A failure surfaces exactly where it is cheapest to fix. It takes several separate live sessions, which is the most allowance-hungry pattern and the most exposed to hitting the free-tier limit partway (a condition the quota-exhaustion sibling governs). A late failure of an early-recorded decision, such as agent registration, can force rework of tasks already done.

No dedicated probe runs. The design is decided and built on Codex's documentation and the curated-marketplace evidence already in the starting state. The four behaviours are first established live by the goal's single end-of-milestone verification run (plugin install, one inline skill, one dispatch of each agent), and any mismatch it reveals is fixed then. It spends the least free-tier allowance: one live session in total, exactly the run the goal already budgets for. Every behaviour-dependent decision stays unconfirmed until the last step. If PLUGIN_ROOT is unset or plugin agents cannot be spawned by name, the fix may reshape the host definition, the agent form, and the dispatch-site wording after all tasks are done. The one run also has to carry both discovery and acceptance. The follow-up-message behaviour is only exercised if the run happens to hit the repair branch.

This rejects the premise that these behaviours need live model runs to be established. Before the dependent questions are answered, the behaviours are settled as far as possible without a model call. Sources are the openai/codex source at the installed 0.159.3 version, and Codex CLI subcommands that call no model: codex plugin marketplace add and codex plugin add on a fixture, codex plugin list, and codex debug prompt-input, which renders the model-visible prompt input and so shows how installed plugin skills and agents are presented. The findings go into the starting state. The goal's end-of-milestone verification run is the only live session. It establishes most of the design-bearing behaviours (skill naming, agent registration, environment set for skill commands) before any decision, at no cost to the free-tier allowance. The source is also more authoritative than the documentation the starting state flags as unconfirmed. Some behaviours may not be settled by source reading or prompt rendering. Whether a finished subagent accepts a follow-up message, and how a model actually resolves a spawn by name, are runtime matters, so those stay unconfirmed until the final run. Reading a large Rust codebase also costs maintainer time and can be misread.

alternative.id: Non-model evidence, then a narrow live probe

open-question.alternative: First, before the dependent questions are answered, the behaviours are settled as far as possible without a model call: the openai/codex source at the installed version, plus codex plugin add, codex plugin list, and codex debug prompt-input on a fixture plugin. Then one small live session on the fixture probes only what that evidence left unsettled, typically follow-up messages to a finished subagent and spawn-by-name resolution. The results go into the starting state before the dependent questions are answered. The goal's final verification run happens at the end. Every dependent decision rests on confirmed behaviour, while the live probe is cut to the minimum the free-tier allowance has to pay for. It is the most up-front work before any requirement is answered: source reading, no-model CLI checks, and still a live session that must be scheduled. Requirements work waits on both. It also still spends allowance on a session separate from the final verification.

open-question.question: The live Codex verification installs the plugin, runs one inline skill, and dispatches each of the two agents once, and both dispatching skills change and commit milestone files in the project they run in. In what project should that verification run?
open-question.alternative: The verification runs in a new, minimal git repository created for the run in a temporary directory outside the cairn checkout. Before any model call, it is seeded without a model by running the milestone-definition tool and the open-question tool directly, so it holds one milestone with one bare open question and one small task. The verification's commits stay in that repository, which is deleted afterwards. The cairn repository keeps only the record the completion procedure writes into TASKS_DONE.md. No seed or run script is kept. It uses the least free-tier allowance of any option. Each Codex session reads a near-empty AGENTS.md and a one-line question and task, not this repository's long CLAUDE.md (AGENTS.md is a symlink to it) and its real milestone files. Nothing the plugin under test does can reach cairn's own history. The evidence goes away with the directory and the seeding steps are not recorded anywhere, so the run cannot be repeated against a later Codex release without working the steps out again. The tiny content may also miss paths that only real-sized questions and tasks reach. It needs a way to install the plugin into a project with no access to this checkout, which depends on the Codex install route question.

The verification runs in a disposable git repository, made fresh for each run from a small seed project kept in the cairn repository: one milestone with one bare open question and one small task, plus the steps or a script that copies it into a temporary git repository and installs the plugin there. Run outputs are thrown away. The seed and the procedure stay committed, so the same verification can be run again for later Codex releases or host changes. It is as cheap and as isolated as a scratch repository, and the verification becomes a repeatable check rather than a one-off. A later maintainer, or a re-run after a Codex update, uses the same inputs without rebuilding them. It adds a maintained, non-runtime artifact to the repository: a nested milestone layout that has to keep up with the file format as later milestones change it, and that the repository layout notes and tests have to account for. Repeating the verification is beyond what the goal asks for.

The verification runs in this cairn repository, on a temporary branch or git worktree, against milestone 40's own live state. It dispatches the alternatives agent on one of the milestone's real bare open questions and the completion agent on one of its real pending tasks. The branch or worktree and its commits are deleted afterwards. Only the result is recorded on main. No seeding is needed, and the agents work on realistic content: real questions, a real requirements.md, and a real task in the project the workflow was built for. Any failure that only shows on real-sized input shows here. It costs more free-tier allowance per dispatch than any small project. Each session loads this repository's long CLAUDE.md through the AGENTS.md symlink, and agents read the real requirements and task context. It needs a suitable bare question and pending task to exist when the run happens. The work the run does is thrown away, and a mistaken checkout or worktree could let its commits land on main.

alternative.id: Cairn repository, kept as real work

open-question.alternative: The verification runs in this cairn repository on main, as actual milestone 40 work. The Codex-run alternatives pass annotates a real bare open question, and the Codex-run complete-all-tasks completes a real pending task. Their commits are kept in the milestone's history like any other run, after review. No allowance is spent on work that is thrown away. Every model call the free tier pays for also moves the milestone forward, and the commits in history are direct evidence that the Codex host does real work on a real project. A plugin that has not been verified writes into the project's real history. Mistaken alternatives or a wrong task completion must be found and reverted, and those commits are later read back by principle capture. The run also has to be timed for when a suitable bare question and pending task exist. It carries the same token cost from the long CLAUDE.md as the discarded-branch option, and whether a run cut short leaves main resumable depends on the quota exhaustion fallback question.

The verification runs in a dedicated, persistent git repository separate from cairn, such as a small sandbox repository under the maintainer's account, seeded once with a minimal milestone (one bare open question, one small task). The run's commits are kept there as lasting evidence, and the repository is reused for later Codex verifications. The evidence lasts and can be inspected (the exact commits Codex made are visible) without adding anything to the cairn repository or touching its history. Content stays as small and cheap as a scratch repository's. It adds another repository, outside the release flow, that only the maintainer can create and keep up, and its seed state goes stale as the milestone file format changes. Keeping the evidence goes beyond what the goal's verification needs.

open-question.question: The live Codex verification runs on a free-tier account whose usage limit may be reached before the plugin install, the inline skill, and both agent dispatches have all been exercised. What should the milestone do if the limit stops the verification partway?

The traffic-badge workflow in each distribution repository pushes with the TRAFFIC_TOKEN secret, a fine-grained token scoped to exactly the three existing repositories and kept in no local copy, so only the maintainer can extend it to uHappyLogic/cairn-codex and set the secret there. How should the milestone treat that maintainer-only step?
